etymology: Greek Gethsemane, from Aramaic for "oil press"; a garden on the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed in agony and was betrayed.
biblical_def: Gethsemane ("oil press") was a garden across the brook Kidron on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord Jesus often resorted with His disciples, and where, on the night of His betrayal, He endured His agony of soul before the cross. Leaving the disciples to watch, He went forward, fell on His face, and prayed, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt" (Matt 26:39). Three times He prayed thus, in such anguish that "his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44), and an angel from heaven strengthened Him. He found the disciples sleeping, and warned them, "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation." There Judas came with a band of men and betrayed Him with a kiss, and there the Lord, in full command, gave Himself up to be taken. Gethsemane stands in the dictionary as the garden of the Savior's agony and submission, where the second Adam, unlike the first in a garden, said, "not my will, but thine, be done," drinking in anticipation the cup of wrath He would shortly bear, and showing forth the perfect obedience by which He set His face to save His people.
webster_summary: A garden on the Mount of Olives (Matt 26:36; Luke 22:39-44) where Jesus prayed in agony before the cross — "not my will, but thine, be done" — sweating as great drops of blood, and was betrayed by Judas.

corruption_summary: Gethsemane needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the real agony and perfect submission of Christ, who said "not my will, but thine," against any denial of His true sufferings or His full obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Suffering-minimized correction. Some so stress the deity of Christ as to make His agony unreal, a mere show. Gethsemane shows the genuine anguish of the God-man, recoiling from the cup of wrath yet submitting to the Father's will, sweating as it were great drops of blood. The dictionary holds the reality of Christ's sufferings: He truly agonized, truly learned obedience by the things He suffered (Heb 5:8), and His submission was no pretense but the costly obedience of a real and willing Savior.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is submission to the Father's will. In a garden the first Adam grasped at his own will and fell; in this garden the last Adam surrendered His will — "not my will, but thine, be done" (Luke 22:42) — and so began to undo the ruin. The dictionary commends His example and His grace: the Savior's perfect submission both atones for our rebellion and teaches His people to pray, in their own dark gardens, that the Father's will, not theirs, be done.
roots_summary: A garden on the Mount of Olives (Matt 26:36; Luke 22:39-44) where Jesus prayed in agony before the cross and was betrayed by Judas; the place of His submission, "not my will, but thine."

etymology: The "high mountain" (traditionally Mount Tabor or Mount Hermon) where Jesus was transfigured in glory before Peter, James, and John.
biblical_def: The Mount of Transfiguration is the "high mountain apart" where the Lord Jesus, about a week after foretelling His death, was transfigured in glory before His three closest disciples, Peter, James, and John (Matt 17:1-9; Mark 9:2-8; Luke 9:28-36). "And he was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light" (Matt 17:2). Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with Him of His coming death ("decease") which He should accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31) — the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to the suffering and glory of Christ. Peter, overcome, proposed to build three tabernacles; but a bright cloud overshadowed them, and the voice of the Father came: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him" (Matt 17:5). When the disciples looked up, they saw "no man, save Jesus only." The Mount of Transfiguration stands in the dictionary as the mountain where the veiled glory of Christ shone forth, a witness that the suffering Servant is the radiant Son of God, that Law and Prophets testify of Him, and that the Father's command is to hear His beloved Son, before whom every other voice must fall silent.
webster_summary: The high mountain (Matt 17:1-9) where Jesus was transfigured in glory before Peter, James, and John; Moses and Elijah appeared, and the Father's voice declared, "This is my beloved Son... hear ye him."

corruption_summary: The Mount of Transfiguration needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the divine glory of the suffering Christ and the Father's command to hear His Son above all other voices.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ-diminished correction. Some reduce Jesus to a mere teacher or prophet among others. On the holy mount His glory blazed forth, and the Father's voice set Him above Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets: "hear ye him." The dictionary holds the unique and supreme glory of Christ: He is the beloved Son, the radiance of the Father's glory, and every other authority — lawgiver, prophet, apostle — bears witness to Him and must yield to His voice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unity of the suffering and the glory of Christ. Moses and Elijah spoke with the transfigured Lord of His coming death; the glory and the cross are not at odds, but the same Christ is the radiant Son and the suffering Servant. The dictionary commends this vision against a faith that wants glory without the cross: the Christ whose face shone as the sun is the same who set His face to die at Jerusalem, and through that death entered into His glory.

etymology: The well near Sychar in Samaria where Jesus met the Samaritan woman and spoke of living water and true worship (John 4).
biblical_def: Jacob's well was an ancient well near the Samaritan town of Sychar, on the parcel of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph, where the Lord Jesus, "wearied with his journey," sat and met a Samaritan woman who came to draw water (John 4:5-7). Asking her for a drink — crossing the deep barriers between Jew and Samaritan, man and woman — He led her from the water of the well to Himself: "whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). He revealed her sin with gentle authority, and then taught the great truth that the hour was come when worship would no longer be bound to Gerizim or Jerusalem: "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" (John 4:24). He disclosed Himself to her as the Messiah, and she, leaving her waterpot, brought her whole town to Him, and many Samaritans believed. Jacob's well stands in the dictionary as the place of living water and true worship, where Christ offered the well of water springing up to everlasting life, taught that God seeks worshipers in spirit and in truth, and made a sinful Samaritan woman the first evangelist to her people.
webster_summary: An ancient well near Sychar in Samaria (John 4) where Jesus met the Samaritan woman, offered the "living water" springing up to everlasting life, and taught that true worshipers worship God in spirit and in truth.

corruption_paragraphs: Worship-misdefined correction. The Samaritan woman raised the question of where to worship — this mountain or Jerusalem. Jesus lifted worship above place to its true nature: God is Spirit, and seeks worshipers who worship Him in spirit and in truth (John 4:24). The dictionary holds that acceptable worship is not a matter of mere location, ritual, or sincerity apart from truth, but of the heart engaged by the Spirit and conformed to the truth God has revealed; the Father seeks such worshipers, and no other worship pleases Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel's reach across every barrier and the living water Christ alone gives. Jesus crossed the divisions of race, sex, and reputation to bring a sinful Samaritan woman to faith, offering the water that springs up to everlasting life. The dictionary commends both: Christ satisfies the thirst of the soul that no earthly well can quench, and He sends the gospel past every wall of hostility to seek and save the lost, even making the convert the first to carry it to others.

etymology: Hebrew, perhaps "house of the ford"; the place beyond Jordan where John baptized and pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God.
biblical_def: Bethabara (called in some texts Bethany beyond Jordan) was the place east of the Jordan where John the Baptist was baptizing when he bore witness to Jesus. "These things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing" (John 1:28). There, the day after his testimony to the priests and Levites, John saw Jesus coming and cried the great words of his witness: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). There he testified that he had seen the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining on Jesus, and declared, "this is the Son of God" (John 1:34). It was from Bethabara that the first disciples — Andrew, and then Peter — began to follow Jesus. Later, when the Jews sought to stone Him, Jesus withdrew again to this place beyond Jordan where John first baptized, and there "many believed on him" (John 10:40-42). Bethabara stands in the dictionary as the place where the Lamb of God was proclaimed, the spot from which the Baptist pointed away from himself to Christ, where the first disciples were drawn to the Savior, and to which the people came in faith, a witness that the whole purpose of the forerunner, and of every faithful witness, is to point men to the Lamb who bears away the sin of the world.
webster_summary: The place beyond Jordan where John baptized (John 1:28) and proclaimed Jesus, "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29); where the first disciples began to follow Christ.

corruption_summary: Bethabara needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the whole purpose of the witness is to point men away from himself to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-promotion correction. The temptation of every gifted servant is to gather a following to himself. John, at the height of his fame, pointed away from himself: "Behold the Lamb of God." The dictionary holds the pattern of the faithful witness: he decreases that Christ may increase, he directs all eyes to the Savior, and he counts his ministry fulfilled not when men follow him but when they follow the Lamb. The forerunner's glory was to be the voice, not the Word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the substitutionary heart of the gospel proclaimed at Bethabara. John named Jesus "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" — the sacrificial Lamb who bears the sin of His people in their place. The dictionary commends this gospel: Christ is the true Passover Lamb, the fulfillment of all the offerings, who takes away sin not by example or teaching alone but by bearing it Himself, and to Him every faithful witness must point the lost.

etymology: From a Semitic root for "springs"; a place near Salim where John baptized because there was much water (John 3:23).
biblical_def: Aenon was a place near Salim where John the Baptist continued baptizing, "because there was much water there: and they came, and were baptized" (John 3:23). The mention occurs in the context of John's last and greatest testimony to Christ. When his disciples came troubled that Jesus was baptizing and "all men come to him," John answered with the magnanimous humility that crowns his ministry: "A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven... He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:27-30). At Aenon, then, the forerunner gladly accepted his own waning as the Sun of Righteousness rose, rejoicing to be the friend of the Bridegroom and content to fade as Christ grew. Aenon stands in the dictionary as the place of John's self-effacing joy, where the Baptist taught that all true ministry is given from heaven and exists to magnify Christ, and where he spoke the words that every servant of God should make his own: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
webster_summary: A place "near to Salim" where John baptized because of much water (John 3:23); the setting of his great word of humility, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).

corruption_paragraphs: Self-exaltation correction. The flesh resents being eclipsed and clings to its own prominence. John, told that his crowds were going to Jesus, rejoiced rather than envied, declaring, "He must increase, but I must decrease." The dictionary holds this as the mark of every faithful servant: the true minister of Christ delights to fade as his Master grows, counts his joy fulfilled in hearing the Bridegroom's voice, and seeks not his own glory but the increase of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all ministry is given from heaven. "A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven" (John 3:27). The dictionary commends John's humility: gifts, fruitfulness, and standing are not achievements to be hoarded but trusts received from God; the servant who knows this holds his ministry loosely, takes no glory to himself, and rejoices to spend it all in magnifying the One who gave it.

etymology: Hebrew, related to shalom, "peace"; the place near which John baptized at Aenon (John 3:23).
biblical_def: Salim was a place near which John the Baptist baptized at Aenon, named in John's Gospel as the landmark by which the location of his late ministry is fixed: "And John also was baptizing in Aenon near to Salim, because there was much water there" (John 3:23). Like several such notices in the Gospels, the precise location is uncertain, but the mention belongs to the closely observed historical record of the evangelist, who anchors the testimony of John in real and identifiable places. It was in this season, near Salim, that John bore his final witness to Christ and spoke the words of his glad self-effacement, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). The name Salim, akin to the word for peace, recalls that the ministry of the forerunner, for all its sternness of repentance, prepared the way for the Prince of Peace, and that John's own peace lay in fading before the rising Christ. Salim stands in the dictionary, with Aenon, as a marker of the place of John's last testimony, a small witness to the historical grounding of the Gospel record, and a reminder that the herald's work, near the place whose name means peace, was to make ready a people for the coming of the Lord.
webster_summary: A place near which John baptized at Aenon (John 3:23); its name akin to "peace," it marks the setting of John's final witness to Christ and a small token of the Gospel's historical grounding.

corruption_summary: Salim needs no defense from redefinition; its incidental mention witnesses to the historical reality of the Gospel record and to John's work of preparing the way of the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Myth-theory correction. Liberal criticism has often treated the Gospels as legend; their incidental, verifiable geography — a place near Salim, chosen for its abundant water — tells against the theory. The dictionary holds the historical reliability of the Gospel record: John wrote what he and others had seen, in real places that could be checked, and such offhand notices are the marks of testimony, not invention.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the forerunner's work of preparing the way. Near Salim, the place of peace, John fulfilled the prophetic word: he was the voice crying in the wilderness, the messenger sent before the Lord (Mal 3:1; John 1:23). The dictionary commends his ministry as the pattern of all true preparation for Christ: calling sinners to repentance and pointing them to the coming Savior, that a people might be made ready for the Lord.

etymology: Greek Dekapolis, "ten cities"; a region of ten Greek cities east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee.
biblical_def: The Decapolis ("ten cities") was a region of largely Gentile, Greek-speaking cities east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, where the gospel of Christ began to reach beyond the Jews even in the days of His earthly ministry. Great multitudes from the Decapolis followed Jesus early on (Matt 4:25). It was in the country of the Gadarenes, within this region, that the Lord healed the man possessed by a legion of demons; and when the man begged to follow Him, Jesus sent him home as a missionary: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee... And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel" (Mark 5:19-20). Later the Lord passed through the Decapolis, healed a deaf man with a speech impediment (Mark 7:31-37), and fed the four thousand in that region. The Decapolis stands in the dictionary as a region of early Gentile-ward gospel advance, a witness that the saving works of Christ were proclaimed among the Greek cities even before the great commission, that a delivered demoniac became the first herald of Christ to a Gentile people, and that the mercy of the Savior was never meant to be confined to Israel alone.
webster_summary: A region of ten Greek cities east of the Sea of Galilee where the healed Gadarene demoniac published Christ (Mark 5:20) and Jesus healed and fed multitudes; a place of early Gentile-ward gospel advance.

corruption_summary: Decapolis needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the early reach of Christ's mercy and gospel beyond Israel to the Gentile world.
corruption_paragraphs: Narrow-mercy correction. Some imagine the mercy of Christ confined to the Jews until after His resurrection. The Decapolis tells otherwise: there the Lord cast out a legion, healed the deaf, and fed the multitude, and a delivered Gentile-region man became the first to publish His works among his own people. The dictionary holds that the compassion of Christ overflowed the borders of Israel even in His earthly ministry, a foretaste of the gospel that would go to all nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the herald's commission given to the rescued. The healed demoniac wished to stay with Jesus, but the Lord sent him to tell his friends "how great things the Lord hath done for thee." The dictionary commends this pattern: those whom Christ has delivered are sent back to their own people as witnesses, and the simple testimony of a changed life — what great things the Lord has done — carries the gospel where the rescued can go and others cannot.

etymology: Hebrew Ephrayim; a city near the wilderness to which Jesus withdrew with His disciples before His passion (John 11:54).
biblical_def: Ephraim was a city near the wilderness, north of Jerusalem, to which the Lord Jesus withdrew with His disciples in the days before His final Passover. After He had raised Lazarus from the dead, the chief priests and Pharisees took counsel to put Him to death; "Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews; but went thence unto a country near to the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim, and there continued with his disciples" (John 11:54). This withdrawal was not from fear, for the Lord had set His face steadfastly toward Jerusalem and would lay down His life of His own accord; rather, it was His sovereign ordering of the time, that He might not be taken before the appointed hour. He had often said, "Mine hour is not yet come" (John 7:30; 8:20); and so He withdrew to Ephraim until the Passover He had chosen for His death drew near, and then went up openly to lay down His life. Ephraim stands in the dictionary as the place of the Savior's withdrawal before His hour, a witness that Christ ordered every step of His passion in sovereign freedom, neither hastening nor delaying beyond the Father's appointed time, and that He laid down His life not as a victim overtaken but as the willing Lamb who chose the very hour of His offering.
webster_summary: A city near the wilderness (John 11:54) where Jesus withdrew with His disciples after raising Lazarus, before His passion; a witness that He ordered the time of His death in sovereign freedom, awaiting the appointed hour.

scriptures: Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews; but went thence unto a country near to the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim, and there continued with his disciples.
...but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come.
No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again...
...Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father...
corruption_summary: Ephraim needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the sovereign freedom of Christ over the time and manner of His death, laying down His life of His own accord at the appointed hour.
corruption_paragraphs: Victim-Christ correction. Some portray Jesus as a tragic victim swept up by events beyond His control. His withdrawal to Ephraim shows the opposite: He governed the timing of His passion, withdrawing until His hour, then going up to die at the Passover He had chosen. The dictionary holds the sovereign freedom of Christ: "No man taketh [my life] from me, but I lay it down of myself" (John 10:18); the cross was not an accident that befell Him but an offering He freely made at the Father's appointed time.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the appointed hour in the life of Christ and of His people. The Lord moved neither too soon nor too late, but according to the Father's set time. The dictionary commends this providence: as Christ awaited His hour in sovereign trust, so His people may rest in the perfect timing of God, who orders every season of their lives, neither hastening nor delaying His purposes, but bringing all to pass at the hour He has appointed.
roots_summary: A city near the wilderness (John 11:54) where Jesus withdrew after raising Lazarus, before His passion; a witness to His sovereign ordering of the hour of His death.

etymology: A covered colonnade on the east side of the temple court in Jerusalem, named for Solomon; a gathering-place of Jesus and the early church.
biblical_def: Solomon's Porch was a great covered colonnade running along the eastern side of the outer court of the temple in Jerusalem, a sheltered place where teachers gathered with their hearers, and a notable setting in the Gospels and the early chapters of Acts. There, at the Feast of Dedication in winter, the Jews surrounded Jesus and demanded plainly whether He was the Christ; and there He declared the security of His sheep — "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand" — and His unity with the Father: "I and my Father are one" (John 10:23-30). After His resurrection and the day of Pentecost, when Peter had healed the lame man at the temple gate, the amazed people ran together to the apostles "in the porch that is called Solomon's" (Acts 3:11), and Peter preached Christ crucified and risen to the gathered crowd. There too "they were all with one accord in Solomon's porch" (Acts 5:12), as the early church bore witness with great power. Solomon's Porch stands in the dictionary as a place of the testimony of Christ and His church, where the Lord proclaimed His oneness with the Father and the safety of His sheep, and where the apostles, after Pentecost, gathered to preach the risen Christ and gather His people in the very courts of the temple.
webster_summary: A covered colonnade on the east of the temple court (John 10:23; Acts 3:11; 5:12) where Jesus declared "I and my Father are one" and where the early church gathered and the apostles preached the risen Christ.

Where the crowd ran to the apostles after the lame man was healed (Acts 3:11).
Where the early church gathered with one accord (Acts 5:12).
scriptures: And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch.
I and my Father are one.

...and they were all with one accord in Solomon's porch.
corruption_summary: Solomon's Porch needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the deity of Christ, who claimed oneness with the Father, and the bold public witness of the early church.
corruption_paragraphs: Deity-denied correction. Some reduce Jesus to a mere man or moral teacher. In Solomon's Porch He claimed full unity with the Father — "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30) — a claim His hearers rightly understood as a claim to deity, for they took up stones to stone Him for blasphemy, "because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God" (John 10:33). The dictionary holds the true and full deity of Christ: He is one with the Father, very God of very God, and no reading that makes Him less than divine can be reconciled with His own words.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is bold public witness. In the very courts of the temple, the early church gathered openly and the apostles preached the risen Christ to all who would hear. The dictionary commends their boldness: the gospel is not a private matter to be hidden, but a public proclamation to be made openly, and the church that knows the security of Christ's sheep and the truth of His deity will not shrink to testify of Him before the world.

etymology: A gate of the temple in Jerusalem where Peter healed the lame man in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 3).
biblical_def: The Beautiful Gate was a gate of the temple in Jerusalem where, shortly after Pentecost, the apostles Peter and John healed a man who had been lame from birth, in one of the first great signs of the early church. "And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple" (Acts 3:2). When he asked alms of Peter and John, Peter fixed his eyes on him and said, "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk" (Acts 3:6). Taking him by the right hand, Peter lifted him up, and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength; "and he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God" (Acts 3:8). The astonished people gathered, and Peter preached Christ to them. The Beautiful Gate stands in the dictionary as the place of healing in the name of Jesus, a witness that the church's true riches are not silver and gold but the power of the risen Christ, that His name still raises the helpless, and that every mercy shown in His name is an occasion to proclaim the Savior who alone makes whole.
webster_summary: A temple gate in Jerusalem (Acts 3:2-10) where Peter healed the man lame from birth — "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk" — and then preached Christ.

Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.

Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: The Beautiful Gate needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the church's true power is not silver and gold but the name of Jesus, by which the helpless are raised and the Savior proclaimed.
corruption_paragraphs: Wealth-as-power correction. The church is often tempted to trust in money and means as the measure of its strength. Peter, who had no silver or gold, possessed something infinitely greater: the power of the name of Jesus to raise a man lame from birth. The dictionary holds that the church's true riches are not material but spiritual; what it has to give the world is not chiefly alms but Christ, and the name of Jesus accomplishes what all the silver and gold in the world cannot.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the saving power and exclusivity of the name of Jesus. The healing was wrought "in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth," and Peter went on to declare, "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). The dictionary commends this confession: it is the name of Jesus, and no other, that heals and saves, and every mercy done in His name is an occasion to point the watching world to the only Savior.
